Issued at 308 AM CDT Sat Sep 19 2026

The trough over the Intermountain West will send a few vort maxima 
into the Central CONUS as we head into Saturday, which will provide 
gradual H5 height falls across the area. The dCVA associated with 
this will continue to deepen a surface cyclone which is beginning to 
expand eastward, with surface pressure falls currently reaching into 
eastern Kansas and eastern Nebraska. The warm front that moved 
through today made into the far northeastern zones of the forecast 
area, and extends into northwest Iowa, while the cold front trailing 
this system is currently positioned from roughly Omaha, Nebraska 
southwestward toward Colby, Kansas as of 08z this morning. Radar 
early this morning is starting to show activity in southeast 
Nebraska and northwest Missouri near the Triple Point, co-located 
with an area of upper-level divergence. Off and on rain showers and 
perhaps some scattered thunderstorms will develop as the day 
progresses through early afternoon, but should remain mostly sub-
severe in our forecast area. Continued low-level southerly flow will 
provide WAA keeping air temperatures in the mid 90s today, with 
dewpoints reaching the upper 60s to lower 70s. The main focus for 
strong thunderstorm activity is favored after 23z this evening, 
mainly along the cold front as the primary forcing mechanism. Ahead 
of the cold front, most of the eastern Plains and lower Missouri 
River Valley will have plenty of daytime insolation that will work 
to destabilize the boundary layer. As the main short-wave trough 
moves overhead, mid-level cooling will promote steeper mid-level 
lapse rates that will pave the path for stronger updrafts, 
especially as this sits on top of warm moist boundary layer. As the 
primary short-wave trough axis moves through, stronger mid-level jet 
streak should help to provide increasing deep layer shear, with 0-
6km bulk values around 30-35 kts, and some deterministic guidance 
does show this overspreading parts of the warm sector and extends 
behind the cold front. This solution is a bit further east than what 
previous numerical model guidance was suggesting the past couple of 
days. Based on 00z HREF guidance, the warm sector appears capable of 
SBCAPE above 1500 J/kg across much of the forecast, with a 
concentrated axis of near 2500 J/kg from near Emporia KS northeast 
toward south-central Iowa, just clipping the Kansas City Metro 
northland. The initial development of the strongest storms is 
expected over Central Kansas after daytime heating. West of the 
forecast area, initial storms will remain discrete, and with some 
directional shear in the first kilometer or two, could see a few 
supercells develop out there. However, by the time strongest 
convergence along the cold front enters our eastern and northeastern 
Kansas Counties, the deep layer shear vector is progged to orient 
more parallel to the boundary and with the low-level jet increasing, 
is expected to result in upscale growth into some kind of QLCS or 
MCS like mode. Depending on the amount of boundary layer mixing that 
occurs and how quickly the front propagates, RAP soundings on the 
warm side of the boundary have been hinting at inverted-v like 
structure below the progged cloud bases, with DCAPE pushing above 
1100 J/kg. This type of environment would favor downburst potential 
with newer updrafts. But then as upscale growth continues, stronger 
cool pool development may lead to strong outflow winds. Current 
expectation is that the large hail threat will mainly be confined to 
areas well west of Kansas City tied to where a supercell storm mode 
is more likely. However, if along the front we have more broken line 
segments and still get new updraft development, the steep mid-level 
lapse rates and healthy CAPE profiles through the hail-growth zone 
may help get hail stones up to around golf ball size. Heading into 
the overnight hours, even after FROPA, another area of mid-level 
height falls will promote additional lift, and is expected to keep 
shower and thunderstorm activity going. While the severe hail and 
wind threat may start to diminish, especially as the front moves 
toward Central Missouri, continued rainfall may augment hydro and 
flooding issues that started earlier this week, especially for areas 
north of the Kansas City Metro that were hit hard this week. HREF 
proability-matched mean QPF values are roughly around 1 inch, but 
there are concerns that these values could be exceeded if this 
boundary stalls. Current deterministic CAM guidance suggests that 
the stronger storms and showers will be fairly progressive enough to 
limit training, with stratiform rain trailing the main system having 
fairly low hourly rainfall rates. With most guidance suggesting that 
showers will start to weaken as they cross into Missouri, have not 
issued a Flood Watch. We will note that some rivers and streams are
